strengths: First volumetric functional maps framework addressing an open problem; mathematically principled extension of surface methods with proper LBO discretization and boundary condition handling
Comprehensive experimental validation across 40-pair ground truth set and multiple benchmark datasets (SHREC'19/20, TOPKIDS) with multiple bases (LBO, CMH, Orthoprods)

Multiple practical contributions demonstrated: spectral connectivity transfer methods, volume-aware surface correspondence (60-68% success on SHREC'20 vs 22-60% surface-only), and dramatic mesh untangling improvement (85% on 1405 previously failed cases)
Rigorous theoretical appendices (B-D) analyzing spectral consistency, isometry preservation between volumetric and surface representations, and boundary trace expressiveness
Seamless integration with existing functional map extensions (CMH, Orthoprods) and algorithmic details enabling reproducibility; code release promised
weaknesses: Limited volumetric dataset availability: validation heavily dependent on tetrahedralizations of surface benchmarks, which introduces topological noise and artifacts (acknowledged limitation in Section 5.4); tetrahedralization itself degrades spectral properties, requiring CMH regularization to compensate

Significant computational overhead (1.01-2.51× slowdown for surface matching) with no consistent practical benefit; full bijectivity in connectivity transfer requires prohibitively expensive 25% of spectrum; MATLAB implementation not production-ready

Connectivity transfer remains incomplete: never achieves bijective maps without external mesh untangling; at 20% spectrum still retains 0.34-0.42% flipped cells (Table 1); acknowledged as 'far from being perfect'

Inconsistent and basis-dependent shape matching results: improvements limited to specific datasets/bases (e.g., VOL dataset benefits only from Orthoprods); SHREC'20 performance reversal when switching from LBO to CMH suggests volumetric signal diluted by numerical artifacts; raises unresolved question of when volumetric information actually helps

Missing fundamental theoretical analysis: authors explicitly state this remains future work; no formal characterization of invariant properties under volumetric maps or principled guidance for basis selection; spectral stability in discrete setting uncharacterized

Insufficient medical validation: single brain segmentation example without quantitative metrics; no comparison with established registration methods (LDDMM, demons) despite medical motivation; limited evidence of clinical utility

Basis selection lacks principled guidance: choice among LBO/CMH/Orthoprods is dataset-dependent; CMH works better but mixes extrinsic information, undermining pure volumetric approach; hyperparameter tuning required per dataset (Appendix H)

strengths: First extension of functional maps to volumetric domains, opening a new research direction
Mathematically sound framework with proper n-dimensional Laplacian discretization and comprehensive appendices providing empirical analysis of spectral stability and theoretical properties
Demonstrates multiple practical applications including connectivity transfer, segmentation transfer, and volume-aware surface matching
Code release and detailed algorithmic descriptions (Algorithms 1-3) support reproducibility
weaknesses: Core methodological novelty is limited: straightforward application of existing functional maps theory to volumetric Laplacian with no new optimization techniques or theoretical insights beyond empirical validation

Severely compromised experimental validation: primary volumetric dataset contains only 40 pairs; standard benchmarks require problematic tetrahedralization of surface meshes, introducing topological artifacts that the authors had to discard in some cases (SHREC'20); systematic bias undermines fair comparison with surface methods

Lacks baseline comparisons with existing volumetric mapping methods (LDDMM, piece-wise approaches); comparisons only against surface functional maps or different basis choices, limiting understanding of practical utility

Inconsistent and marginal improvements: on SHREC'20 performance depends critically on CMH basis (existing method [73], not a contribution), VOL dataset shows degradation (1.88e-6 → 2.92e-6), success rates vary from 14.84% to 60% depending on dataset, raising question of when volumetric approach is preferable to surface methods
Significant computational overhead (1.01x-2.51x slowdown) with minimal accuracy gains, and paper lacks memory analysis or scalability discussion for industrial-scale meshes
Connectivity transfer incomplete: achieving fully injective maps requires 25% of spectrum (computationally prohibitive); authors acknowledge this as limiting factor

Lack of theoretical analysis: no convergence guarantees, error bounds, or invariance properties for volumetric functional maps; authors acknowledge theoretical study is future work, undermining fundamental motivation

Limited quantitative evaluation of applications: segmentation transfer shows only qualitative results without standard metrics (Dice scores, Hausdorff distances); connectivity transfer and solid texturing lack rigorous validation

Method sensitivity to mesh quality acknowledged in appendices but remains practical concern; discrete LBO stability depends on vertex position and density, exacerbated in volumetric setting with larger neighborhoods

Incomplete technical justification: rationale for Neumann boundary conditions, choice of cotangent formula over alternatives, and when volumetric vs. surface representation is preferable not clearly established

strengths: First extension of functional maps framework to volumetric (tetrahedral) domains - a genuine novelty filling a significant gap in volumetric correspondence literature

Rigorous mathematical foundation with thorough theoretical justification: proper LBO discretization, spectral analysis, isometry preservation studies, and control-theoretic proofs of linear independence
Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple datasets (40 mesh pairs with ground truth, SHREC'19/20, TOPKIDS, medical imaging) with honest reporting of limitations
Novel technical contributions including two elegant connectivity transfer approaches (transfer and extrapolation) leveraging boundary traces of eigenfunctions
Demonstrated practical impact: 85% improvement in mesh untangling algorithm success rate, applications in segmentation transfer and digital fabrication
Seamless integration of existing functional map techniques (ZoomOut, CMH, Orthoprods) showing the method's generality
Excellent presentation with clear exposition, effective visualizations, extensive appendices with theoretical justification and algorithmic details
Honest discussion of limitations, failure modes, and open challenges (dataset scarcity, computational costs, tetrahedralization dependency)
weaknesses: Limited volumetric dataset availability: only 40 mesh pairs with identical connectivity for primary validation; heavy reliance on tetrahedralized surface data rather than native volumetric meshes; had to discard 2 SHREC'20 meshes due to tetrahedralization artifacts
Significant computational overhead for shape matching (1.01×–2.51× slowdown, Table 2) due to additional interior vertices; scalability to large modern volumetric meshes unaddressed
Strong dependency on tetrahedralization quality: SHREC'20 results require CMH basis to compensate for topologically introduced noise; suggests method sensitivity not fully characterized
Basis size vs. injectivity trade-off: 5% basis yields ~4.6% flipped tetrahedra; 25% needed for full injectivity, creating tension between quality and computational cost

Shape matching improvements are inconsistent and basis-dependent: VOL dataset shows minimal improvement without Orthoprods; SHREC'20 shows worse performance with standard bases (Table 2); gains appear to come from additional volumetric information rather than methodological superiority

Limited theoretical insight: paper provides empirical justification but lacks analysis of what geometric properties are preserved under volumetric functional maps; authors acknowledge this as needed future work
Medical imaging validation insufficient: only 2 brain shapes demonstrated for segmentation transfer; Fig. 8 shows residual noise issues; motivation is strong but application validation is shallow
Shape matching results overstatement: claim that volumetric approach 'consistently outperforms surface-only methods' is not fully supported by mixed results in Table 2 and Appendix H
Comparison fairness concerns: tetrahedralized surface datasets may artificially benefit volumetric methods; comparison with LDDMM-based and learning-based volumetric methods missing
